title: Before we ask students to belong, we should ask where
summary: Billy Wong and Zach Spire look at how the spaces of university signal who belongs, and who is expected to already know the rules
full_text:
Every September, universities try very hard to make sure that students, especially new students, feel welcomed.

There are induction talks, tours and welcome fairs. These events are designed to help students find their way into university life and feel a sense of belonging.

But belonging doesn’t only happen in welcome week. It’s not settled in the early stages of university life. Belonging is worked out slowly, in the ordinary spaces students move through, in daily life both on and off campus.

Belonging is spatially organised

Many universities approach student belonging with a focus on students’ friendships, social groups, confidence and how much they feel accepted. These things matter. But more attention is needed to how the spaces of the university shape students’ understanding of their belonging.

By spaces, we do not only mean buildings, although physical space is important. Buildings, pathways, libraries, cafés and lecture theatres shape how a campus is organised, navigated and experienced. But university space extends beyond the material. We propose attending to how belonging is spatially constructed through physical, digital, relational and structural spaces.

There is a dialogue when students enter these spaces. What can they do? Can one sit down? Can one speak, or stay? How should one behave? How does one learn the rules of the room?

Some of these rules are explicit, but others are implicit and bound up in power and authority relations. They can also operate online through what forms of participation are visible and valued.

If belonging is about whether students feel they matter and can make sense of their place in the institution, then space is one of the ways that message is communicated. Some spaces say “come in and stay.” Others say “move along,” “this is not for you,” and “you need to already know the rules.”

The rules of the room

Take the library as one example. In our earlier research, it served multiple purposes. In addition to providing resources for learning, it was also a space for social networking, conversations and study groups.

Even within the library, there are different zones with different expectations. Some rooms are for group work. Others are for quiet study. Some spaces have fewer explicit rules, meaning students can talk and chat. So even within one building, the rules of space governs how students are expected and allowed to behave.

For example, a group of friends may take over an entire table, but there may still be two unoccupied seats. Those seats are, in theory, available to all. But they may feel unavailable to someone who does not want to question that implied social barrier.

The same applies to digital space, including student portals, virtual learning environments, lecture recordings, discussion forums and support systems.

These spaces can also shape belonging. A student may be able to hear the lecture and see the slides in an online class, but still miss the informal conversations, group dynamics and sense of being in the room.

The hidden hard work of space and belonging

For commuter students, there are very specific aspects of their lives that may or may not fit with how university spaces are designed. There is the travel time involved. Once they arrive, if there is a big gap between teaching, where will they go? Where can they rest? Where can they work without spending money?

This is different from students who live close to the university, who can go back to their residence and relax before returning to teaching. For commuter students, space plays a big part in shaping belonging, inclusion and exclusion.

There are other students where space will shape experiences: minority ethnic students in spaces dominated by particular groups, disabled students, students in halls who may still feel isolated, and students with work, care, faith, financial or health-related commitments. Proximity does not ensure meaningful connection.

This is why presence is not the same as participation. A student can be on campus and still have nowhere they feel able to stay, take part or belong.

From welcome week to the whole institution

Universities invest considerable time and energy to develop and deliver their welcome week, and rightly so. A campus tour can show students where the library is, where to find support and give them a “feel” for the university’s physical layout. But rarely does it tell students how those spaces work in practice. Where can students go if there is a two-hour gap between classes? Where can they sit or rest without spending money? Online, students may be shown where to login, but not necessarily how the different systems, portals or websites fit together. The tacit rules of university space can be made more explicit.

But spatial belonging does not end with induction. Universities ought to ask who is using their spaces, who is not and why. Which spaces are the hot and cold spots? Are spaces intended for student use being used as envisaged?

Universities should review regularly how students actually make use of university spaces, beyond whether they are simply available. This might include looking at opening hours, timetable gaps, places to “hang around” and the ease of navigating their digital systems.

Belonging is therefore not only the work of induction, student support or engagement teams. It is also shaped by estates, timetabling, teaching, digital infrastructure, commuting patterns and informal social space.

All of this links to our Leverhulme Trust-funded project. The study will explore how students experience different university spaces and what this tells us about belonging, inclusion and exclusion.

Students do not live inside welcome week. They live in timetables, teaching rooms, digital platforms, libraries, cafés, corridors and the gaps between formal provision. They often live in the spaces between our words. If universities want students to belong, they need to ask not only how students are welcomed, but where they are expected to belong and whether those spaces are available to them.

title: Why has the OfS downgraded graduate outcomes?
summary: Stephen Isherwood explains that despite the challenges of measuring career outcomes, they remain central to student interests, value for money and informed choice
full_text:
The Office for Students (OfS) has reduced the importance of employment outcomes metrics within its quality framework, citing that employment outcomes are influenced by factors beyond universities’ control and that Graduate Outcomes data is imperfect.

But if students are expected to take on significant financial risk when choosing higher education, can regulators justify stepping back from measures of what happens after graduation?

The Ford problem

Ford generally make good cars and in the 1980s and 90s Ford was the market leader.

So, if you were in the market for a new family car in 1990 you could assume that buying the just launched Mark V Escort was a pretty safe purchase. It wasn’t, I drove one, it was a dud.

Prospective buyers quickly worked out they shouldn’t rely on the Ford badge to indicate quality in the case of the Mark V Escort as everyone across the industry panned it. Car nerds at the time like me read about three car magazines a week.

In the end, Ford had to invest heavily in upgrading the Mark V and within two years had significantly improved its quality and sales recovered.

Hidden outcomes

What has this to do with graduate outcomes data and B3 requirements?

Take a look at the employment outcomes data across a range of specific courses on the Discover Uni website and you may be surprised just how often this message pops up:

There was not enough data to publish information specifically for this course. This may be because the course size is too small or not enough students responded to the survey. This does not reflect on the quality of the course.

In cases like these prospective students have to rely on summary data that represents a much broader range of courses, and of course the marketing materials designed to promote the course.

The OfS has published the outcomes of their consultation on their future approach to quality regulation. Part of the review focused on what is called the progression indicator in Condition B3. For those that aren’t that interested in the minutia of university regulation, this is the part of the regulatory framework that is supposed to ensure that the sector is delivering for students.

Here is a reminder of what the OfS is supposed deliver on, note the reference to careers, progress and value for money:

We aim to ensure that every student, whatever their background, has a fulfilling experience of higher education that enriches their lives and careers.

Our four regulatory objectives. All students, from all backgrounds, and with the ability and desire to undertake higher education:

are supported to access, succeed in, and progress from, higher education

receive a high quality academic experience, and their interests are protected while they study or in the event of provider, campus or course closure

are able to progress into employment or further study, and their qualifications hold their value over time

receive value for money.

The overall report is 89 pages long, but for simplicity I’ve pulled out two paragraphs that summarise the OfS’s position: “There were high levels of support for the removal of the requirement for providers to meet a minimum threshold for progression, generally because respondents agreed that the factors affecting employment outcomes are complex, and that these are less directly under the control of the provider than whether a student continues or completes their course” and “Some of those who supported its removal also commented on perceived weaknesses in the Graduate Outcomes Survey (GOS) data, such as the response rate achieved…”

The OfS approach

It is no surprise that many institutions would rather not be held to account for graduate employment outcomes.

Universities control their marketing campaigns, admissions processes, course delivery and marking structures, but career outcomes are much harder to influence. Influencing employment outcomes is a complex undertaking and does require investment over time.

The Graduate Outcomes survey itself has been managed in a way that has seen response rates fall from 52 per cent to 32 per cent over the last four years (The Destinations of Leavers from Higher Education was imperfect, but when universities managed this themselves response rates were over 80 per cent).

Instead of pushing to increase response rates and thereby the data available to students, the OfS is using the low response rates as a reason to remove career outcomes as a performance measure.

Fix the data, not the metric

The fact that the UK has a loose link between subject studied and career options compounds the need for strong outcomes data – Institute of Student Employers (ISE) data shows that over 80 per cent of employers do not specify subject studied when recruiting.

I’m going to pick on law as it is relatively easy to get the stats, but the same applies to the majority of disciplines. In 2022 there were 5,953 training contracts or barrister pupillages available with employers, yet 26,290 students were accepted onto law degree courses.

These numbers become more dramatic when you consider that many law firms recruit students who have not studied law. This is not to say “don’t study law,” but prospective students should be made aware of the implications of their choices.

Diluting B3 measures may seem an attractive option to the sector. But if we are going to have a system of uncapped course numbers where students’ choice is the dominating factor, then they should have the information and consumer rights resources to inform and protect them.

The B3 conditions are conditions for registration, they are not trivial. By watering down the very performance measures designed to enhance student outcomes, the Office for Students is not acting in students’ interests, which in the long run will only harm the reputation of the sector.

title: Book review: Reclaiming Purpose – The University in an AI World by Paul LeBlanc

The post Book review: Reclaiming Purpose – The University in an AI World by Paul LeBlanc appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This review was kindly authored by Mary Curnock Cook CBE, a Trustee of HEPI.

The book’s author Paul LeBlanc is the former President of Southern New Hampshire University, where he led its transformation into the largest non-profit provider of online higher education in the US. He’s a visiting professor at Harvard University Graduate School of Education.

I have just re-read this wonderful book some eight months after Paul LeBlanc kindly shared a preview copy with me. It says something about how quickly the world is changing when I compare the notes I jotted down back in January to those I made this time. Or perhaps it was me that changed? There was something about that first reading that gave me a more settled and confident understanding of the sheer breadth of challenge that AI brings to higher education’s most deeply embedded assumptions.

Back in January, I was captured by Paul’s invitation to higher education to

dream again, to see itself not only as a transmitter of expertise but as a builder of a better society

and to see AI not as a monster but

a powerful force that requires us to be more human, more intentional, and more courageous than we have ever been

But in the intervening months, we’ve seen attitudes shift against screens in general and AI in particular. Consider headlines like ‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’ (Katerine Rundell in the Guardian), and analysis in the Economist showing that the question of how AI will shape society has become politically explosive in the US. It would be tempting for higher education to set all the traffic lights to red and get everyone back to the exam hall.

But even as the ground has shifted, Reclaiming Purpose does not ignore or belittle such debate. Rather it is a heartfelt call, as the title suggests, for universities to reclaim their purpose, to transition from an

inefficient, inequitable engine of knowledge transfer into a global system of human development, committed to equipping [people] with the wisdom, skills, and ethical compass needed to navigate and shape the Age of AI

Paul emphasises how the extraordinary potential of AI requires us anew to emphasise our humanity, reclaim an elevated societal role, curate human connection, develop moral imagination, embrace the ensouled self and instil in graduates the orientation and capacity for human flourishing. It is genuinely inspiring stuff.

LeBlanc is not primarily interested in academic misconduct, institutional efficiency or the practicalities of integrating AI into teaching and assessment. Instead, he asks what higher education should exist for if machines increasingly perform many of the functions that universities have traditionally helped students master. His answer is that universities must shift their centre of gravity from epistemology to ontology: from what students know to who they become.

Nevertheless, the book does not hold back from setting out the fractures in the higher education model which have been further exposed since the advent of generative AI.

In his chapter ‘the idea of the university revisited’, Paul sets out three cultural shifts that have been needed for a long time but are now more urgent. The first is in what we value. The prestige of universities may have relied on the mastery of knowledge for centuries, with human skills like empathy, teamwork and leadership assumed to emerge as a mere byproduct of campus life. Instead, he calls on the sector to recognise the primacy of such skills (he rightly decries the term ‘soft skills’ as signalling secondary or peripheral importance). He says:

[A] graduate’s ability to mediate conflict or navigate cultural difference should be seen as just as important as their ability to parse thermodynamics or analyze primary sources.

The second shift is surfacing the hidden curriculum of

social interactions that are incubators and sometimes crucibles [to] develop character and skill.

Currently, he points out, this is largely left to chance, “unaided by intentional design”. A new culture, he says, would treat these opportunities for human skills development not as accidents but as subjects of serious teaching and learning.

They would be named, taught, and assessed, not merely hoped for.

The third required shift is away from traditional disciplinary silos, recognising that the development of human skills requires integrative learning and collaboration across disciplines where “human and technical demands intermingle”.

The book describes in some detail the idea of precision learning (as opposed to merely personalised learning), based on work that Paul did with other colleagues to build a platform that precisely times learning interventions based on more than just past academic performance or VLE ‘events’. This section is of value in elucidating what AI is capable of, although such a specific product solution feels slightly at odds with his discussion of the wider dysfunctions of higher education. He also sets out a significant shift in the role of faculty to become more human and more relational so that students feel more viscerally that they really matter. While the AI handles basic scaffolding and content generation and delivery, faculty’s focus moves to learning experience design and high-touch mentoring, asking them to learn to love students again.

While delving into the potentially harmful and seductive nature of technology that simulates human voice and tone, his section on anthropomorphism reminds us that thanking our LLM makes no more sense than thanking the toaster. Beneath the humour lies a serious concern that students may increasingly form relationships with AI systems that mimic care without genuinely caring.

True to his roots, he returns often to how AI (and precision learning) could democratise access to higher education to less wealthy populations such as those in sub-Saharan Africa or in refugee camps, shifting relative scarcity to abundance of access.

Central to LeBlanc’s thesis is the emergence of a “care economy”. As AI increasingly performs routine cognitive work, he argues that societies will need many more people working in teaching, healthcare, social care, mental health and other relational professions. Universities, therefore, should be preparing graduates not only for work but for human-centred work. Reclaiming Purpose faces head on the fact that students want higher education to prepare them for meaningful careers and a ‘choice-filled life’. But his perspectives on how the workforce will change in the AI era perhaps rest on too blunt an assumption that professional white-collar jobs will disappear and that consequently displaced workers will flock to the care economy if only these professions are better valued and better paid.

The book is more sure-footed in reimagining the post-secondary education ecosystem. As well as the shift from epistemological to ontological teaching, the degree itself, as a single static credential, is challenged as Paul sets out a vision for learning as a lifestyle, with lists of courses and programmes replaced by a ‘knowledge graph’. He says that

a traditional syllabus is a rigid list of stations you must visit in order. A knowledge graph is a subway map that shows every station, every transfer point, and every possible route. You can start at any station and see all the different paths, or pre‑requisite skills, required to get to a new destination.

While the metaphor is powerful, I won’t be the only one reflecting on how elusive an effective system of credit accumulation and transfer has proved to be in UK higher education. Similarly, his reminder that data readiness is the most significant barrier to effective AI deployment in higher education will bring many readers back down to earth.

Despite Paul’s assertion that higher education is “broken and ripe for disruption”, this is no futurist dismantling of the status quo. Rather, Paul’s warm, engaging and humorous style draws the reader into a world where AI could be the precursor to universities reclaiming their moral orientation and becoming “the architects of a profoundly human future”. At a time when much discussion of AI in universities focusses on productivity gains and plagiarism, Reclaiming Purpose asks a more profound question: if AI assumes much of the work of knowledge transfer, what then becomes the distinctive role of universities? Can higher education credibly claim the mantle of human flourishing?

title: Schools not ready for AI and 'crying out' for government guidance, report warns
summary: Author Sir Anthony Seldon says AI needs to be addressed with the same urgency as a war or epidemic.
full_text:
Schools are "crying out" for guidance from government on how pupils and teachers can use AI safely and effectively, a new report has warned.

Sir Anthony Seldon, former head teacher and author on AI in education, says the technology is being used more and more frequently, but that its introduction has been "chaotic and anarchic".

His report calls for the government to roll out a national framework for adopting AI in education in England, including training teachers on how to use it, which schools should use to develop their own "AI strategies" by September next year.

The government says its changes to the curriculum in England will give children digital skills and help them spot disinformation.

Sir Anthony's report, co-authored with venture capitalist Tim Bunting, says schools have not been prepared for AI's arrival.

Sir Anthony co-founded the group AI in Education, which was set up in 2023 to help educational institutions navigate AI safely.

His report argues that getting a grip of AI requires the same level of national urgency as wars and epidemics, and requires a taskforce modelled on the one which helped to roll out the Covid vaccine.

The report recommends a 10-point plan for AI in education in England, including:

The prime minister delivering a landmark speech to set out the importance of aligning education with how AI is used in the real world

Schools and colleges developing their own AI strategies, and having Ofsted assess their implementation as part of its inspections

A mass information campaign to set out the opportunities and risks of AI

Using AI to transform the way schools and colleges collect and use data to track pupil progress

Reforming assessments into a "two-lane" system of both exams and a "continuous evaluation of a student's understanding" using AI

The report says its poll of young people suggests many of those who responded thought AI was making education less important in their lives, with some saying it could eventually replace teachers and make universities "useless".

"Put simply, education has not kept pace with how – and how much – young people are already using AI, and that gap is starting to show up as a loss of perceived value in the institution itself," the report says.

A spokesperson for the Department for Education says ministers take the "significant opportunities and challenges" of AI "incredibly seriously".

As well as refreshing the curriculum in England, they say they are building new AI tutoring tools and introducing new vocational routes to get children into successful careers.

Some schools have already embedded AI into the curriculum. Benjamin Barker, principal at King's Leadership Academy in Liverpool, says he wants his students to learn how to use tools safely, while also developing their critical thinking skills.

Student Emma, 12, says she uses AI for her robotics projects, as well as proof-reading her English homework, and believes more students should be taught how to use it responsibly.

"AI is coming into the future. It's getting more advanced," she says.

"There's no way we're going to completely pull back from it. So I think that we should use it to be better people."

title: Catching the Greased Pig
summary:
Catching the Greased Pig
Sara Brady Mon, 09/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

Readers respond on the “kinda, sorta” requirement.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
Last week I wrote about the frustrating dilemma of how to respond when a student fails a corequisite developmental course but passes the simultaneous credit-bearing course. In a purely academic sense, it seems like a no-brainer to waive the developmental coreq, but that raises tricky financial aid issues. But making it optional runs into Kay McClenney’s accurate observation that students don’t do optional. Every time we think we’ve found a solution, it slips away, like the proverbial greased pig.

Happily, I have the best readers ever, so I put out a call for solutions. Folks stepped up. Not every answer would work in my context, but contexts differ, so here goes.

A few readers suggested a lecture/lab model, as in introductory science classes:

That would work for capturing the students who need the developmental one, but it would add time and cost for students who don’t. Admittedly, this model was the way that DeVry taught composition in the late ’90s; I remember teaching “writing lab” in a room full of oscilloscopes. In states with hard caps on credits for associate degrees—New Jersey, I’m looking at you—the added credits would wreak havoc on curricula.

A reader from the Virginia Community College system offered this:

I’ll admit liking this one. It puts the instructor of the developmental class in an awkward spot, but if they know that going in, and it’s a matter of policy, it could work. It also leaves the students who placed out of the developmental class unburdened, which is a plus. The fact that this apparently works at the level of a statewide system within shouting distance of D.C. offers some assurance that the financial aid issues aren’t prohibitive.

A reader from a math department offered a parallel observation:

This makes sense institutionally, but it feels a bit dishonest to the students. Hidden prereqs are a real thing, but the term is usually used pejoratively; they make degree completion look faster and cheaper than it actually is. On the bright side, keeping those courses out of the degree path does answer the question of what to do if a student fails the lower-level course. Still, this feels a bit slippery to me.

Another reader offered a pass-fail option as a workaround:

Pass-fail makes a lot of sense to me in the context of a developmental course. And framing this as retroactive credit-for-prior-learning has a certain logic to it. It comes close to the Virginia system solution, which inspires confidence.

We’ve occasionally discussed mandatory tutoring as an alternative. One reader offered:

The end of that quote is a bit of statistical inside baseball, but I’m intrigued by the idea that once students go to tutoring, they’ll go back voluntarily. Local experience has largely suggested otherwise. I’m curious whether there’s research more broadly on whether going to tutoring works like the first potato chip—you can’t have just one—or if more students see it as something closer to going to the dentist. The concept of required tutoring makes a great deal of sense to me, but if students skip it, we’re right back where we started.

As long as we have open admissions, we’re going to have challenges like these. Students show up with different academic backgrounds, and sometimes they follow pathways of their own devising. It’s worth remembering that that’s good. Our challenge is to meet the needs of a wide range of students within the confines of minimal resources and a financial aid system based on full-time, residential students. It’s not a clean fit.

But thank you to all of the wise and worldly readers who wrote in! You’ve made suggestions that we haven’t considered locally and confirmed my sense both that a lot of people care, and that there are more possibilities in this world than are considered in my philosophy. Thank you!

title: When Accreditation Becomes Everything, It Stops Being Accreditation
summary:
When Accreditation Becomes Everything, It Stops Being Accreditation
Elizabeth Redden Mon, 09/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

A proposed Department of Education rule would change the purpose of accreditation and risk rendering it less effective.

Byline(s)
Nasser H. Paydar
full_text:
If the lights go out in your house, you call an electrician. If a pipe bursts, you call a plumber. Both matter. Both protect the house. But asking the plumber to inspect the wiring does not make the house safer. It simply gives the plumber the wrong job.

Something similar is happening in American higher education.

The U.S. Department of Education’s proposed Accreditation, Innovation and Modernization regulations begin with goals that many of us share: stronger accountability, better student outcomes, less unnecessary regulatory burden, greater innovation and better protection for students and taxpayers. The Council for Higher Education Accreditation and the colleges and universities we represent support those goals. Our members are deeply committed to student success, educational quality, accountability and continuous improvement.

But good goals do not guarantee good policy.

The question is not whether higher education should be accountable. It should be. The question is who should be accountable for what and how.

I have spent most of my professional life in higher education. I have been a faculty member, an academic administrator and a university chancellor. I have also served inside the U.S. Department of Education, and today I lead CHEA. Seeing higher education from all three perspectives has reinforced something I have come to believe deeply: Strong accountability does not require everyone to do the same job. It requires each participant to do their own job well.

That principle has long been embedded in American higher education. Institutions are responsible for educating students and fulfilling their missions. The federal government determines whether institutions meet requirements for participation in federal student aid programs. States authorize colleges and universities to operate. Independent accrediting organizations evaluate academic quality through peer review. These responsibilities sometimes overlap, but they are deliberately distinct. Congress chose this structure rather than creating a federal system for determining academic quality.

Those distinctions are not bureaucratic trivia. They are safeguards. Yet several provisions in the proposed regulations risk blurring them.

Should an accreditor be responsible for determining whether a university complies with every applicable federal and state law? Institutions must, of course, obey the law. So must accreditors. But determining whether the law has been violated is the responsibility of the government agencies charged with enforcing it and, ultimately, the courts. Turning accreditors into legal compliance officers does not strengthen accreditation. It changes its purpose.

Should an accreditor determine whether a university has spent too much on faculty, facilities, student services or scholarly activity? Accreditation should certainly examine whether an institution has the resources necessary to fulfill its educational mission. But requiring accreditors to conduct cost-benefit analyses of institutional spending places them in the very different role of judging how universities allocate their resources. Those decisions appropriately belong to institutions and their governing structures.

These new responsibilities also carry real costs. Requirements imposed through accreditation ultimately translate into additional data collection, documentation, analysis, reporting and review. Before adding new requirements, policymakers should ask whether they are justified by a meaningful improvement in quality and student protection.

And should Washington prescribe exactly how accreditors evaluate student achievement, academic freedom, intellectual diversity, faculty policies and other dimensions of academic life?

These are important issues. CHEA strongly supports academic freedom and meaningful attention to student outcomes. But supporting an objective is different from believing that the federal government should prescribe what an independent accreditor must measure and how it must conduct that evaluation. The proposed rule too often crosses that line.

There is an important distinction here: Federal oversight of accreditation is necessary. Politicization of accreditation is not. That distinction matters, especially now.

Higher education is being asked difficult questions about cost, value, student success, public trust, academic freedom and workforce preparation. Accreditation cannot respond to those questions simply by defending the way things have always been done. It must continue to improve. It should use better information, focus more clearly on student outcomes, reduce unnecessary burden and encourage innovation.

But reform should strengthen accreditation’s ability to judge educational quality, not gradually transform it into an enforcement mechanism for every public policy objective affecting higher education.

Indeed, the more responsibilities we pile onto accreditation, the greater the danger that it becomes less effective at fulfilling the responsibility for which it was created.

In its formal comment to the Department of Education, CHEA identifies provisions it supports and recommends revisions where the proposal would expand accreditation beyond its appropriate role. Higher education does not need less accountability. It needs smarter accountability. A safe house needs working plumbing, reliable electricity and a sound structure. Every part matters. But that does not mean the plumber, electrician and contractor should all be asked to do the same job.

Let institutions remain responsible for fulfilling their missions and serving their students. Let government enforce the law. Let states exercise their authority. Let institutions govern themselves within those boundaries. And let independent accreditors carry out their role within the framework Congress established: evaluating educational quality while helping to protect students and support institutional improvement.

The electrician and the plumber both matter. We should resist the temptation to hand them the same toolbox.

title: Under New Loan Limits, Students Struggle to Finance Final Year
summary:
Under New Loan Limits, Students Struggle to Finance Final Year
jessica.blake@… Mon, 09/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

Evolving guidance from the Education Department shut two students out of federal student loans. “It really feels like someone’s stabbing you,” one mom told Inside Higher Ed.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
Twelve days out from the start of her senior year at Texas Christian University, Kaylee Webb was still waiting for a $19,000 Parent PLUS Loan that would help pay for tuition, fees, room and board at her dream school—as it had every semester so far. But the loan never came.

“I’d started sending emails to the financial aid office saying, ‘Hey, why does it not show up for the parent loan?’” but to no avail, recalled Webb, a computer information technology major. “By Aug. 13, I hadn’t heard anything. So I went to speak with them in person. They were just like, ‘Sorry, you’re not eligible.’”

This fall marks the first academic year since sweeping changes to federal student loans took effect in July, including a limit on the previously uncapped Parent and Grad PLUS loans. Webb and other existing borrowers didn’t think they would be affected because of a legacy provision outlined in the law, as well as the Education Department’s final rule, which was released in April. But then ED clarified its interpretation in early August.

“We thought we had everything under control with finances,” said Kaylee’s mom, Katrina Webb, a middle-class accountant who closely followed the evolution of the loan-limit rules.

A TCU official told them that based on that August clarification, legacy access was no longer calculated by the length of time a student was enrolled, but the number of credit hours they had completed. Since Kaylee had exceeded the minimum number of credits hours for her degree—120—she was no longer protected.

In a statement to Inside Higher Ed, the university said that while it never wants to see a family “negatively impacted,” the “subsequent administrative guidance and rulemaking from the Department of Education changed how loan eligibility is determined.” (ED has said the clarification didn’t represent a change in policy.)

Half of Kaylee’s credits came from an associate degree that she earned in high school in an effort to save money. Katrina said she was “devastated.”

“It really feels like someone’s stabbing you when you have a child that tried so hard to do all the right things to make her dream come true,” she said. “I’ve talked to several other parents, and all of their kids brought in transfer credits. These are all kids that tried to get ahead, and now they’re being punished. I don’t think that’s fair for any of us when we’re trying our best.”

But not all colleges see the department’s clarification, delivered via a webinar, as binding. And even groups like the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators say they can’t provide blanket advice and are encouraging institutions to consult with their own legal counsel.

Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles told Inside Higher Ed that it would stick to the department’s final rule and base loan eligibility on years enrolled, not credit hours, as that is the “current written interpretation.”

“LMU is aware of the Department of Education’s discussion of a different interpretation during its August [webinar] and is awaiting formal written guidance from the Office of Federal Student Aid before making any changes to its financial aid policies,” a spokesperson said in an email.

That decision left Kathryn Cook, a business owner and student, without the Grad PLUS loan she needed to pay for the last of four years in LMU’s evening law program—though she expected ED’s clarification would help.

When the rule was first drafted, Cook was told she was in the clear. But that changed in July. The law school also has a more standard three-year J.D. program, and according to an updated notice from LMU, the department told colleges they must use “the full-time program length,” or, in this case, the shorter three-year program, to calculate a student’s remaining eligibility for unlimited loans.

Cook had already borrowed up to the new $257,500 lifetime limit—so further federal loans weren’t an option.

When she heard about the webinar’s change to credit hours, she thought she’d found a saving grace. But six weeks later, Cook still hasn’t heard a formal update from the Loyola aid office, though she did find out about their decision via the university’s statement to Inside Higher Ed. Her fall tuition is past due, and her account is on a registration hold for the spring semester.

“It’s becoming really stressful for me. Because I have a huge chunk of my budget missing,” Cook said. “At this point, I’m struggling to pay my rent. And my mom is trying to support me, but she’s a widow. She’s trying to retire. And I’m a first-generation student, so my mom doesn’t really have those resources.”

While the specifics vary, Webb and Cook are among thousands of students who are facing loss of eligibility, delays in getting federal funds or other challenges as financial aid offices across the country grapple with changes to the federal loan system.

The Education Department and colleges faced a tight timeline to roll out the new policies after they were passed in July 2025 as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. As a result, experts say, financial aid offices have scrambled to interpret evolving guidelines, which have caused immense confusion among students and, in some cases, left families uncertain how they will pay for the remainder of their students’ degrees.

The Education Department said in a statement that it has provided and continues to provide “ample support to financial aid administrators,” including sessions at multiple financial aid conferences as well as published guidance, Q&As, webinars, office hours and podcasts.

“Not only did the Department implement these regulations on the July 1 statutory timeline, but we published the package two months in advance, providing additional time for schools to prepare,” said Ellen Keast, a department spokesperson.

‘Rules Change Along the Way’

At Saint Louis University, students and families have inundated the financial aid office with calls and emails, asking about the loan changes.

Alex DeLonis, assistant vice president of student financial services, said his office received 5,000 calls—the same call volume SLU experienced during the bungled launch of the new Free Application for Federal Student Aid in 2024. Emails, he said, followed a similar pattern.

“We thought FAFSA simplification might have been an anomaly … but to have two pieces of legislation that have completely flipped things upside down and we’ve had to implement so closely together—it’s just a lot,” DeLonis said. “It’s hard to predict and plan when the rules change along the way.”

SLU is providing stopgap solutions like supplemental and emergency grants and loans to help students whose loan access has been curtailed by the new rules. But not all colleges can do that, and even for those that can, it’s not a long-term solution. And students like Webb and Cook who’ve learned they no longer have access to PLUS loans aren’t the only ones experiencing confusion. Some still have access to PLUS loans for now but are confused about how much time they have left. Others are struggling to understand a proration provision, which ties how much a student can borrow to the number of credit hours they are taking. And then there’s the ongoing uncertainty over what counts as a professional degree.

On top of that, some financial aid offices had to manually update their software systems or make calculations by hand in order to carry out these changes, since the software providers themselves haven’t been able to catch up with ED’s guidance.

Combined, these obstacles have often delayed the disbursing of loans, even for those who are eligible.

“What we hear … is a general sense of anxiety that the rules are shifting faster than the financial aid system can keep up,” said Mike Pierce, executive director at Protect Borrowers, a student advocacy organization. “The student loan system and America’s higher education finance system are really not built to handle this kind of change.”

Karen McCarthy, vice president of federal relations at NASFAA, said the compounding challenges trace back to two root causes: the complexity of the bill and the time crunch the department had to implement it.

“What we are seeing now is the impact of not following that master calendar,” McCarthy said, referring to the department’s typical schedule of finalizing rules by Nov. 1 so that colleges have time to implement the changes the following academic year.

But Keast noted that an advisory committee signed off on a draft of the changes in November 2025. “If institutions waited until the final rule was issued to start preparing, that was their decision,” she said. (Financial aid administrators weren’t part of that committee.)

Feeling ‘Abandoned’

After a few weeks of uncertainty, Kaylee Webb’s plans for her senior year are back on track. Now, a full month into the fall term, she’s received her class ring and is planning for senior pictures.

“I’m still super ecstatic to be graduating from TCU,” she said. “Like I said, it’s the only place I wanted to go, and it’s the little things along the way that help lighten the mood.”

But for a little bit, she “didn’t know if I was going to be able to graduate. It was like my world was crashing down.” And even now, the solution isn’t ideal.

With the help of TCU financial aid, the Webbs found a private loan program run by the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board called the College Access Loan. Kaylee had a part-time job and a strong enough credit score to qualify for the loan on her own; if that hadn’t worked out, her parents could have been co-signers.

“As a parent, I was trying to keep all the loans that I could out of Kaylee’s name,” Katrina said, adding that private loans don’t have the potential for loan forgiveness like the federal ones do.

Still, at the end of the day, her daughter will be able to graduate. She’s working hard to boost her résumé and hopes to secure a job that will pay off the debt.

Private loans aren’t an option for everyone, like Cook.

She’s trying to stay optimistic and search for other options, but if nothing changes she’ll have to take a leave of absence. She could still become a recognized attorney by finishing her studies under the California bar’s apprenticeship program, but she hopes she doesn’t have to go that route.

“I’d still be having to pay for a degree that I never got,” she said.

And while the Webbs and Cook said they can sympathize with the department and their financial aid offices, whose staffers had to operate on a short runway, they’re still frustrated by their circumstances.

“I feel really kind of abandoned, especially from the lack of communication. It’s worn me out,” Cook said. “It’s just so unjust. I feel like I need to continue telling people how it’s affecting me so they can fix it.”

title: Campus Tours Have Never Been Bigger
summary:
Campus Tours Have Never Been Bigger
Johanna Alonso Mon, 09/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

As it becomes increasingly evident that getting a student to visit campus is one of the best ways to convince them to enroll, colleges are overhauling their tours.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
Rides in shiny, branded shuttles. Personalized parking spots and goodie bags. Free flights and hotel rooms across the country. Multithousand-dollar scholarships, and multimillion-dollar welcome centers.

These are some of the ways colleges and universities are investing in campus tours and visits, in the hopes that new and improved experiences will convince more prospective students who visit to eventually enroll.

Campus tours have long been an important way for institutions to capture the interest of students and parents. But during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Americans broadly weren’t traveling or attending in-person events, some campuses launched virtual versions of their tours, raising questions about whether in-person tours would become obsolete.

Six years on, families and institutions alike seem to agree: In-person campus visits are more important than ever. Today’s juniors and seniors, were in elementary school when COVID-19 shut down their schools, leaving much of their generation with social deficits and, in some cases, mental health struggles, whose impact still lingers. That means the amorphous campus vibe—the pure energy of a normal day on campus that every tour seeks to capture—carries special weight.

“As a high school student, their knowledge and their perspective is really oftentimes limited to that which they can find—guides, rankings, U.S. News reports,” said Matthew Lysne, an Oregon-based lawyer who took his daughter, now a freshman at a small liberal arts institution, on a cross-country college tour last year. “She had ideas about” where she wanted to go, he said, but “the thing that she thought would matter most ended up not being [as important]. And it was tours that ended up revealing that.”

Studies have found that whether a student visits campus is one of the strongest predictors of their matriculation. Tours are even more valuable for smaller campuses; in a summer 2026 survey conducted by Niche, a college rankings company, 92 percent of enrollment leaders at small colleges cited the campus visit as the single most important strategy for securing an incoming class.

That’s why some institutions are focused on jazzing up their tours.

Take Hofstra University. When admissions and enrollment leaders realized it was impossible to show the entire 244-acre New York campus in a single walking tour, they invested in an old-fashioned trolley, complete with wooden seats and decked out in Hofstra’s blue-and-gold color scheme, to take visitors on a scenic trip through campus at the start of every tour. The innovation is as much about helping save prospective students’ feet from getting sore as it is about conveying Hofstra’s brand.

“The trolley is as charming as all of the trees—we are an arboretum—and that trolley kind of reflects the charm of our campus,” said Jessica Eads, senior vice president for student enrollment, engagement and success at Hofstra.

Enrollment leaders at several campuses told Inside Higher Ed that efforts to improve their tours have fueled student interest and led to major year-over-year increases in the number of tours they conduct annually; at Albion College, a small liberal arts institution in Michigan, tours have increased by about 23 percent since 2022, the first year after COVID-19 that in-person tours reached normal levels. At John Carroll University, a Jesuit institution in Ohio, they’ve increased by 46 percent over that period.

“When you’re trying to make the decision about the institution that’s right for you, you can read as much as you want about it, or you can see that big school football game day atmosphere on TV,” said Mandy Konkle, vice president of enrollment management at Albion. “But actually being on campus, surrounded by the people that are going to be in classes with you, that are going to be teaching you—that gives you that feeling in your gut that tells you it’s the right place.”

Changing Priorities

Campus tours have been around since the Vietnam War, when four-year colleges began competing in earnest with community colleges; before then, according to a 2011 Slate article on the history of the practice, students occasionally visited college campuses, but not in an organized way.

Still, the campus tour of 60—or even 20—years ago bears little resemblance to today’s. For one, students need vastly different information now than they did even at the turn of the 21st century. Pre-internet, students learned details like student-to-faculty ratios, cost of attendance and majors offered during information sessions on campus visits; now, that information is readily available online, and students use the visit mainly to gain a sense of the campus. Academic priorities are also shifting; students and families are more concerned than ever about the return on investment of their degree.

But what exactly do today’s students want out of their campus visits?

One thing a swath of institutions have landed on is personalization. That doesn’t just mean swag emblazoned with their names—though that’s part of it. Trinity University in Texas told Inside Higher Ed that students attending tours have VIP parking spots set aside for them by name. Meanwhile, when a student begins a tour at Baylor University, a spire in the welcome center lobby lights up with their name, plus what they want to be when they grow up.

The ability to have a specialized experience on the tours … helped my daughter visualize what her life would really be like.”

—Matthew Lysne, parent

In some cases, personalization means individualized tours focused on what a given student is interested in seeing instead of a set route. Institutions including the University of Dayton and Albion offer one-on-one experiences, where each student is paired with a tour guide who shares their prospective major—or perhaps an extracurricular interest or where they went to high school.

That connection between tour guide and prospective student is key, enrollment leaders said, because it allows the student to ask specific questions about their experience that other guides might not be equipped to answer.

Tour guides at Marquette University in Wisconsin are given a short fact sheet about upcoming visitors so they can choose the best fit for themselves. Zachary End said he gives tours not only to visitors who are interested in one of his three majors—psychology, cognitive science and economics—but also to undecided students, because he, too, started Marquette unsure what he wanted to study.

“I tend to relate to those students better,” he said. “I think being able to talk about how, when you come here, you don’t have to have that figured out, and I didn’t have that figured out, and I’m in a really good space—it’s something that puts not just the students on tour at ease, but it also really puts the families at ease.”

One-on-one tours aren’t new to Marquette, but as demand for tours has increased, the campus has had to hire more tour guides to maintain that ratio, according to Kate Bracciano, director of admissions visits and special programs.

The Rise of Add-Ons

Colleges are also expanding what they include in tours. Some institutions, like Trinity, allow prospective students and their families to select “add-ons” to their tours—additional experiences such as sitting in on a class, eating lunch with a current student or meeting with a particular faculty or staff member.

Tours that offered such add-ons made the biggest impression during Lysne’s tours with his daughter.

“The ability to have a specialized experience on the tours … helped my daughter visualize what her life would really be like,” he said. “So, at one school, she [got] the chance to see the honors college and honors dorm, and a student going to that school in the honors college is going to have a drastically different college experience than someone who’s not … and that was really helpful for her, and it [was] a very big selling point for her on that college.”

Marquette, meanwhile, has begun giving prospective students an opportunity to dive deeper into their academic interests through specialized visits to academic departments, where they can meet with faculty—many of whom have received training about how to talk about the university with visitors, Bracciano said.

“We shared with them some high-level information from different reports of, here are the things that Gen Z is looking for in a campus visit. Here are the questions that families are going to come with that you should be prepared for. You should have someone ready to greet the family—really trying to help them build a structure around those visits and understand strategies or practices to really engage that family in the visit,” she said.

Some colleges are also sponsoring visits for students who may not have the means to travel. Mount Saint Mary’s University in Los Angeles pays for flights and lodging for out-of-town students attending certain events, such as scholarship interviews and Admitted Students’ Day. Marquette has flown in admitted students and their families from markets beyond the Midwest since 2022, with the program growing each year; last spring, 318 families participated. John Carroll sends buses to bring local high schoolers to attend events on campuses.

Hofstra University, on Long Island, meanwhile, takes a slightly different approach: The university flies in college counselors from across the country for an overnight visit so they can learn about the institution firsthand.

As another incentive to convert tour attendees into enrolled students, some colleges also offer application fee waivers or even scholarships to students who visit campus. Albion College provides $2,000 per year, or $8,000 total, for example, to any enrollee who took a tour.

“We decided to do this because we know that students aren’t going to choose us if they don’t see us, and so it’s important to get as many students to campus as possible,” said Konkle. “So while $2,000 may not seem like a lot to some families for one year, $8,000 over the course of four years is important.”

Back to Basics

To make a positive first impression, some colleges are redesigning or erecting new visitor centers on campus. John Carroll, for one, is creating a brand-new welcome center in its administrative building, changing “what used to feel like a large conference room” into “more of a community space,” said Mike Andelbradt, assistant vice president for enrollment and director of admission. “We were going [for] coffee shop–meets–museum, so a lot of soft seating, beautiful furniture. The space is actually an old Jesuit dining room from when our campus was originally founded.”

Trinity University, too, is launching a new welcome center as a sort of “grand entrance” to the university, according to Dean of Admissions Justin Doty, who said the project was first conceptualized a decade ago. Opening in November, the space is tailored to prospective students and will house the institution’s admissions department, but it will also serve as a hub for other members of the campus community. That dual purpose is by design, Doty said: “Any time you put food and drink in any space, it’s going to be activated with current students. So, I think the synergy is actually going to be really cool, to have prospective students and our current Trinity students kind of bumping into each other.”

You want the visit to feel effortless, for there to be no hiccups, no issues. People don’t realize on the back end all of the work that went into making it appear effortless.”

—Alicia Taylor, associate director of admissions at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville

Not every tour innovation has to be pricey or flashy, though. Enrollment leaders also talked about attention to detail; things like cleanliness, landscaping and tour guide expertise all play a huge role in a prospective student’s experience. Institutions have taken steps to improve the visual appeal of their campuses specifically to improve tours; at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, for example, the chancellor of the university took a tour himself just to spot the imperfections, Alicia Taylor, SIUE’s associate director of admissions, told Inside Higher Ed.

Following his tour, “they completely changed the face of our quad area on campus; everything’s branded. We have beautiful flowers now, everywhere around campus,” she said. “It just feels like a more cohesive, thoughtful kind of space.”

Colleges have also worked to cultivate star teams of customer service representatives, from the front desk workers in the admissions office to the tour guides themselves. At Trinity, being a tour guide is one of the best-paid on-campus jobs, and administrators believe that investment helps them recruit the most knowledgeable and charismatic students, Doty said.

Faced with mounting pressure to bolster enrollment, many college leaders seem aligned on one point: Few expenses are too big—and no detail is too small—when it comes to crafting a flawless campus tour.

“You want the visit to feel effortless, for there to be no hiccups, no issues,” said Taylor. “People don’t realize on the back end all of the work that went into making it appear effortless.”

title: 5 MLAs, including former leader, returning to B.C. Conservative caucus as prospect of election looms
summary: Former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford and MLA Scott McInnis are among those who have accepted invitations from Doerkson to rejoin the troubled caucus.
full_text:
Interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson is moving to repair ruptures in the Opposition that saw 13 legislators quit caucus or be expelled by former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who stepped down on Sunday.

In a statement issued Monday afternoon, Doerkson said the Conservative Caucus of British Columbia had readmitted former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford and MLAs Scott McInnis, Linda Hepner and Claire Rattée.

Rustad says in a statement that his "time as leader is over" but not his service to the province.

The Nechako Lakes MLA also says "high level" unity talks are underway between the Conservatives and the breakaway CentreBC party, and rated the chance of success at 95 per cent.

The developments come after the caucus of B.C.'s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election in light of Findlay's resignation, raising the prospect of voters going to the polls while the Opposition has no fixed candidate to become premier.

An interim leader is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis, but Rustad says there is a way for Doerkson to become premier.

Rustad told a news conference at the legislature that there were "obviously lots of people" in B.C. who don't know the Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator, but he called Doerkson a "quality individual" and said he would be happy to have him lead the party into an election if he wanted.

Rustad said of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell needed to "let politics go."

He said Clark and Campbell were among the "players" trying now to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and they should realize that "their time is over."

"That may mean time is over for me, too. I don't know," said Rustad. "But I'm not going to be trying to force my will or my vision in terms of what our party was … onto whoever the new leaders are going to be," he said.

"If they want me to be part of that in terms of supporting and building, I will do that. But it is time for that older generation of politicians to step aside."

Rustad provides timeline

In a statement later Monday that confirmed he had accepted Doerkson's invitation, Rustad said talks between CentreBC and the Conservatives should succeed and the province "cannot afford two opposition parties" with an election looming.

Findlay's resignation followed weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, including the ejection of Rustad and two others on Friday.

He provided a timeline of the chaos the preceded that moment.

Rustad said he asked Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was "emotion and frustration around the table."

The next day he got a text from Findlay expelling him. Fifteen minutes later that was rescinded.

But on Friday he was told he was out.

Speculation about a snap election being called, less than two years since the 2024 election, intensified Monday when the NDP announced that cabinet minister Lana Popham won't be running for a sixth term.

"After 17 years as the MLA for Saanich South, I have made the difficult decision not to seek re-election,” she said in a statement.

The minister of agriculture said her decision not to run again was difficult and sad.

Popham's statement came after NDP MLAs met Sunday night to discuss Findlay's departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators, instead of just those on the government benches.

"I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the B.C. Conservatives," the email obtained by The Canadian Press said.

It went on to say the meeting was to "to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team," an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Premier David Eby's former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

The Canadian Press briefly attended the meeting, along with at least two Conservative legislators, before being asked to leave.

Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be "election ready."

McInnis releases statement

McInnis, who represents Columbia River-Revelstoke, had quit the Conservative caucus on Sept. 2, saying he did not agree with the direction of Findlay's leadership.

Unlike other colleagues dissatisfied with Findlay, McInnis did not join CentreBC under their leader Peter Milobar.

McInnis said in a statement on Monday that the opportunity to return "home" came at a critical time for the province.

He rejected the need for "ideological purity tests" and said the prospect of a provincial election made a united opposition more important than ever.

No party had ever defeated the B.C. NDP without being a "big tent party," he said.

McInnis said he never lost respect for his Conservative caucus colleagues, with whom he shared a "common belief that British Columbians deserve practical solutions, fiscal responsibility, and a government focused on delivering results."

Turmoil in the Conservative ranks, who have been divided over ideology and direction, birthed the CentreBC party which picked up eight legislators last week, including Milobar.

All are former Conservatives, including seven who quit that party's caucus in recent weeks, while Eleanor Sturko was ejected by Rustad last year.

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the B.C. Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before crossing the floor to join the Conservatives and being reelected in 2024.

title: Conservatives criticized for appointing Ont. mayor as byelection candidate
summary: The federal Conservative party is being criticized over its decision to appoint a candidate for an upcoming byelection, instead of holding a nomination contest.
full_text:
The federal Conservative party is being criticized over its decision to appoint a candidate for an upcoming byelection, instead of holding a nomination contest.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre surprised many when he announced at a rally on Sunday that Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis will be the party's candidate in Brantford-Brant South.

The seat is vacant now that Larry Brock has returned to his job as a Crown prosecutor, but a byelection hasn't been called yet. On Friday, Brock said he resigned from the House of Commons, after five years as the MP for Brantford-Brant South.

Brock endorsed Dave Carrol, a local pastor who had hoped to run in a nomination race that he learned on the weekend will not happen.

Carrol says he's "deeply disappointed" by the decision and adds he also had the endorsement of former MP Phil McColeman.

In a Facebook post, Carrol said that on Sunday he learned that "one candidate has been appointed rather than selected through the nomination contest that so many of us had been preparing for. I wish Kevin Davis well, but I would be less than honest if I said I wasn't deeply disappointed."

Carrol said "The grassroots tradition of this party is what drew me to it nearly two decades ago, and I've spent those years helping build it here… knocking on doors, getting memberships, raising money, supporting our candidates and trusting local members to make good choices. I hoped that same grassroots tradition would guide the process when I finally put my own name forward"

In a statement, the Conservative party says it wanted to ensure a candidate was ready to hit the ground running and that Davis was "overwhelmingly endorsed" by people who attended Poilievre's rally on Sunday.

The House of Commons is scheduled to return from its summer recess on Sept. 21.

title: When does being ‘apolitical’ become a political act? An ethicist on the Ed Sheeran saga
summary: Being ‘apolitical’ sounds like being neutral – but it isn’t. Can Macklemore’s removal from the Loop tour over his ‘free Palestine’ stance be defended at all?
full_text:
Headlines this week have been inundated with news of artist Macklemore being dropped from Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour, following Macklemore’s onstage calls to “free Palestine”.

The rap artist said Robert Kraft, owner of New England Patriots and the Gillette Stadium, barred him from playing in his stadium, and rallied other stadiums to join the boycott.

In response, Sheeran’s remaining support acts also withdrew. Sheeran has attempted to distance himself from the decision, suggesting it was the promoter’s and not his. He has taken an “apolitical” stance, referring back to his history of avoiding public political statements.

But the resulting condemnation from fans and commentators suggests forcing neutrality in such situations isn’t straightforward.

What does it mean to be ‘apolitical’?

Politics isn’t limited to government. In a more general sense, it refers to the relationships of power in society and between members of society, and efforts to change them.

This seems to be what Ed Sheeran’s recent statements are reaching for. He claims to be apolitical in the sense that he keeps his political views separate from his work as an artist:

People buy my records to put on while they make out. I’m not Mr Political. I vote the way I feel I should, but won’t tell somebody else what to do.

Importantly, Sheeran’s recent statement doesn’t just claim he is apolitical on the issue of Palestine, but that he is apolitical in general. This would require never expressing any views in relation to the arrangement of power and control in society.

It doesn’t seem Sheeran has done this. He has previously supported campaigns against Brexit and far-right racism, has supported Jermey Corbyn, and played a Concert For Ukraine in 2022. These are political positions.

So, if Sheeran is not apolitical at all times, this means he chooses to be apolitical on specific issues. In this case the issue is Palestine.

Is apolitical the same as neutral?

Being apolitical is not the same as being “neutral” on political issues, especially in cases where significant injustice is taking place.

Some argue attempts at neutrality on such issues entrench, or at least permit, the injustice.

Beyond the entertainment industry, neutrality has often been a question in the context of wars. Here, the importance of weighing intention against outcomes become especially clear. The Red Cross argues its political neutrality allows it to assist more people affected by conflict.

On the other hand, mercenary soldiers – who are politically neutral and fight purely for wages – are generally seen as much less ethical. Many current conflicts in the world are fought by such soldiers.

The 17th century philosopher Grotius argued that because mercenaries fight for pay, without regard for the justice of their cause, “there is no course of life more abominable and to be detested”.

Yet some advocates argue that if mercenaries result in faster ends to a conflict, that outcome may make their actions ethical – though their intentions may not be ethical.

Is it unethical to be apolitical?

Not always. Being apolitical is defensible based on some philosophical perspectives, but context matters.

Greek philosopher Epicurus argued politics is best avoided. He believed we should aim for “tranquility of the soul”, retired from the affairs of the world, and living one’s life in peace.

It seems possible to be “neutral” – to not hold views – on specific political issues. Yet many philosophers, including Aristotle and Italian philosopher Antonio Gramsci, have held that humans are unavoidably political creatures. As such, some issues seem to demand a response from us.

Philosopher Hannah Arendt showed it was a kind of “thoughtlessness” that facilitated the evils of the Nazi regime: a failure to pay attention to serious ethical wrongs.

In Sheeran’s cases, perhaps from a personal perspective he does think he is being “apolitical”. However, his decision takes place in a broader context, wherein it appears to have been influenced or made by wealthy individuals with well-stated political stances on Palestine.

He has gone beyond simply refusing to express his own political beliefs. He has allowed Macklemore’s political views to be removed at the behest of another party acting in its own political interest, thereby favouring one over the other.

Action through inaction

Another problem with choosing not to “take sides” on a particular issue is that it is often a response reserved for those who are privileged enough to not be affected by the injustice or power relationship under discussion.

At the same time, the more privileged we are, the more ability we have to affect change. This is one of the justifications Macklemore offers for his support of Palestine.

Sheeran’s removal of Macklemore from his tour is a statement on whose interests count, and who has the power in this situation. And that’s political whether he wants it to be or not.

title: Exclusive: Iran's school year opens as fees triple and enrolment falls
summary: As Iran’s academic year begins, families face severe strain from doubling tuition fees, soaring stationery prices, war fears and a plunging currency. Euronews Persian spoke to Iranians about declining enrollments and deep economic distress across the country.
full_text:
Iran's new academic year opens on Wednesday against a backdrop of tuition fees that in some cases nearly tripled over the summer, with enrollment falling at private schools across Tehran as war fears, sanctions and the continued collapse of the rial squeeze family budgets.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian marked the start of the academic year by ringing the school bell at a girls' primary school in Tehran on Monday.

The Ministry of Education has instructed schools to prioritise in-person teaching after periods of online learning during previous phases of the war.

The ministry also issued a directive capping tuition increases at private schools at 35% for the new academic year, setting fees across the country at between 14 million and 145 million tomans (€53–€549). In practice, the cap is not being observed.

Bita, a final-year high school student in eastern Tehran, told Euronews she paid 80 million tomans (€303) last year and 220 million tomans (€833) this year — a 175% increase.

"I'm in my final year of high school. Students in lower grades pay somewhat less. We also have to pay a separate fee for pamphlets and school-printed textbooks, which comes to around 20 million tomans (€76)," Bita said.

"Right now, for a senior at a private high school, their family has to pay roughly 250 million tomans (€947) for their education. Of course, in the affluent neighborhoods in the northern part of the city, this cost goes even higher," she explained.

Although the rial is Iran’s official currency, everyday pricing and transactions are conducted in tomans — where 1 toman equals 10 rials — with the open market rate on Monday standing at slightly over 264,000 tomans (or 2,640,000 rials) per euro.

Maryam, 57, works as an accountant at several private primary schools in southern Tehran.
